clinicalPearls: A slow-growing mycobacterium with fastidious requirements: it needs iron-supplemented (haemin-containing) media and a lower incubation temperature of around 30 to 32 degrees Celsius
The laboratory must be alerted to the possibility, because routine media and standard temperatures fail to recover it
Causes skin lesions, characteristically papules, nodules, and ulcers over the cooler extremities and overlying joints, in immunosuppressed patients
Septic arthritis and osteomyelitis may accompany the skin disease, and disseminated infection occurs with severe immunosuppression
Recognised in transplant recipients, patients on tumour-necrosis-factor inhibitors, and people with advanced HIV
In otherwise healthy children it is a cause of cervical lymphadenitis
Management combines multidrug antimicrobial therapy with reduction of immunosuppression where possible and surgical excision for lymphadenitis
reference.pathophysiology: Mycobacterium haemophilum is a slow-growing mycobacterium with a distinctive requirement for iron (haemin) and for lower incubation temperatures, reflecting its tropism for the cooler superficial tissues. The presumed environmental reservoir is water. Disease overwhelmingly affects hosts with impaired cell-mediated immunity, in whom the organism produces granulomatous skin nodules and ulcers over the limbs and joints, sometimes with underlying septic arthritis or osteomyelitis and, in the most immunosuppressed, dissemination. In immunocompetent children the same organism can localise to cervical lymph nodes. Its fastidious growth requirements mean infection is frequently missed unless specifically sought.
additionalDifferentials: Other nontuberculous mycobacterial skin infection (M. marinum, M. chelonae)
Disseminated fungal infection with skin nodules
additionalInvestigations: Skin or tissue biopsy for histology and mycobacterial culture
Culture on iron-supplemented media at a lower incubation temperature after alerting the laboratory
Molecular identification to species level, sometimes required when culture fails
MRI for suspected septic arthritis or osteomyelitis
Assessment and optimisation of immune status and immunosuppressive medication
Blood cultures and staging for dissemination in severely immunosuppressed patients
redFlags: Disseminated disease in a severely immunosuppressed host
Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis requiring surgical management
Rapid progression in transplant or anti-TNF-treated patients
Failure to grow the organism despite strong clinical suspicion, indicating the need for specialised media
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends heavily on the degree of immunosuppression and how quickly it can be reversed. Localised lymphadenitis in children does well after excision, whereas disseminated disease in profoundly immunosuppressed patients can be difficult to control and carries a worse prognosis.
pitfalls: Not alerting the laboratory, so appropriate media and incubation temperature are not used and cultures are falsely negative
Failing to reduce immunosuppression as part of treatment
Attributing skin nodules to another cause and delaying biopsy
Treating osteoarticular disease medically without surgical input
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
ATS/IDSA guideline on nontuberculous mycobacterial diseases
management: Alert the laboratory to culture on iron- (haemin-) supplemented media at a lower incubation temperature, as routine conditions fail to recover the organism and delay treatment
Treat with prolonged multidrug antimycobacterial therapy, typically a macrolide such as clarithromycin combined with a rifamycin such as rifabutin and a fluoroquinolone such as ciprofloxacin
Reduce and optimise immunosuppression where possible, tapering tumour-necrosis-factor inhibitors or minimising transplant immunosuppression
Debride skin lesions surgically and manage accompanying septic arthritis or osteomyelitis with combined medical and surgical care
Treat childhood cervical lymphadenitis with complete surgical excision
Stage for dissemination with blood cultures and imaging in profoundly immunosuppressed patients and monitor treatment response
Refer to infectious diseases, recognising that outcome depends heavily on how quickly immunosuppression can be reversed
